panels.title: Interactions per day

targets.rawSql:
SELECT date_trunc('day', occurred_at) AS time, count(*) AS interactions
FROM assistant_facts WHERE $__timeFilter(occurred_at) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

panels.description: AI assistant usage. One row per turn, keyed by message_id, so a redelivered event converges instead of inflating this line.

panels.title: Questions by outcome

targets.rawSql:
SELECT date_trunc('day', occurred_at) AS time, outcome AS metric, count(*) AS turns
FROM assistant_facts WHERE $__timeFilter(occurred_at) GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1

panels.description: Asked vs answered. Only `answered` answered anything: a refusal and a no_match are honest replies, and folding them in would make the rate rise as the assistant got less useful. Grouped, not hard-coded, so a new outcome appears on its own.

panels.title: Response time (ms) — generated vs cached

targets.rawSql:
SELECT date_trunc('hour', occurred_at) AS time,
  avg(duration_ms) FILTER (WHERE cache_tier = '') AS generated,
  avg(duration_ms) FILTER (WHERE cache_tier <> '') AS cached
FROM assistant_facts WHERE $__timeFilter(occurred_at) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

panels.description: Split on purpose. The blended mean drifts with the cache hit rate rather than with the system getting faster, so it describes neither experience. The whole turn, retrieval included — a provider-only number would flatter us.

panels.title: Recommendation acceptance (window)

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE accepted) AS accepted,
  count(*) AS turns_naming_items
FROM (
  SELECT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM order_item_facts i
    WHERE i.user_id = a.user_id AND i.menu_item_id = ANY(a.item_ids)
      AND i.placed_at >= a.occurred_at AND i.placed_at < a.occurred_at + interval '24 hours'
  ) AS accepted
  FROM assistant_facts a
  WHERE $__timeFilter(a.occurred_at) AND a.user_id <> '' AND cardinality(a.item_ids) > 0
) s

panels.description: Scored PER TURN, not per item: one answer naming five dishes is one recommendation a customer acts on or does not, and per-item scoring would cap a perfect answer at 20%. Matched on what the answer CITED, inside 24h.

panels.title: Conversion after an interaction

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM order_facts f
    WHERE $__timeFilter(f.placed_at) AND f.user_id <> '' AND EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM assistant_facts a
      WHERE a.user_id = f.user_id AND a.user_id <> ''
        AND f.restaurant_id = ANY(a.restaurant_ids)
        AND f.placed_at >= a.occurred_at AND f.placed_at < a.occurred_at + interval '24 hours'
    )) AS attributed_orders,
  (SELECT coalesce(sum(f.total_cents), 0) / 100.0 FROM order_facts f
    WHERE $__timeFilter(f.placed_at) AND f.user_id <> '' AND f.settled_at IS NOT NULL AND EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM assistant_facts a
      WHERE a.user_id = f.user_id AND a.user_id <> ''
        AND f.restaurant_id = ANY(a.restaurant_ids)
        AND f.placed_at >= a.occurred_at AND f.placed_at < a.occurred_at + interval '24 hours'
    )) AS attributed_revenue

panels.description: Counted ORDER-side and distinct: three questions about one restaurant followed by one dinner are one order, and the revenue beside it must not be tripled. Revenue is settled money only. Correlation within a window — not a controlled measurement.

panels.title: Engagement

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  round(count(*)::numeric / nullif(count(DISTINCT conversation_id), 0), 2) AS turns_per_conversation,
  count(DISTINCT user_id) FILTER (WHERE user_id <> '') AS customers
FROM assistant_facts WHERE $__timeFilter(occurred_at)

panels.description: Depth and reach. Returning customers are counted by distinct CONVERSATIONS, not turns: a long conversation is one visit that went well, two conversations are two occasions the assistant was worth opening. The empty user_id is excluded, matching the API's `_people()`: assistant_facts.user_id is NOT NULL with '' for anonymous, so counting it distinct makes every anonymous turn one synthetic extra customer — and the dashboard and the API would answer the same question differently.

panels.title: Grounding — candidates vs dropped

targets.rawSql:
SELECT date_trunc('hour', occurred_at) AS time,
  sum(candidates) AS candidates_retrieved, sum(ungrounded) AS dropped_ungrounded
FROM assistant_facts WHERE $__timeFilter(occurred_at) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

panels.description: What the validator dropped before the answer shipped. A rising line means retrieval is feeding the model things it cannot support — the leading indicator for AssistantUngroundedAnswer, which fires on what got through.

panels.title: Time to first token (NFR-21: p95 < 1.5s)
panels.description: What a customer feels. A streamed answer's HTTP duration is its connection LIFETIME, which is why stream routes never enter the HTTP latency histogram.

panels.title: Answer latency by task (NFR-21: generate p95 < 6s)
panels.description: Split by task: `explain` is templated and fast, `generate` is a model call. Averaging them lets the fast path hide the slow one.

panels.title: Cache hit rate by tier (NFR-24)
panels.description: Load-bearing, not an optimisation: at the ceiling provider quota is the binding constraint and this is what keeps generations inside it.

panels.title: Provider failovers & refusals
panels.description: The degradation ladder, visible. One failover is the design working; a sustained rate means the primary is down and every answer pays the retry first.

panels.title: Knowledge freshness (NFR-28: p99 < 60s)
panels.description: Committed menu change -> visible to retrieval. A stale index does not fail loudly: it answers confidently about a menu the kitchen has already changed.

panels.title: Interaction-fact consumer lag
panels.description: The panel that decides whether every panel ABOVE it can be trusted. If this projection stalls nothing errors — the charts keep rendering and quietly describe a shorter window than their label claims.

panels.title: Cost per order (budget $0.004)
panels.description: NFR-25's first-class line. Orders is the denominator, not turns: a cost-per-turn improves simply by having fewer turns. Prices come from the llm-costs.yml table — never from this panel — so the dashboard and the tripwire alert read the same source. Budget derivation: capacity-plan §7. Bounded with `< 1`: with assistant spend and no placements in the window the ratio records +Inf, and one infinite point makes the whole range unreadable against the budget line.

panels.title: Spend rate by model and direction
panels.description: USD per hour. Split by direction because the two halves are controlled by different knobs — a context cap bounds prompt tokens, max_output_tokens bounds completion — so a rise on one side names its own fix.

panels.title: Unpriced tokens (the cost line's blind spot)
panels.description: Tokens billed by a model with no row in the price table. Anything here means every cost number on this dashboard is CONFIDENTLY LOW rather than visibly broken: the unpriced model drops out of the join and the panels keep rendering a smaller number with no gap in it.

panels.title: Projected spend / 30d at the current rate
panels.description: A straight extrapolation of the current rate, not a forecast — it moves with traffic and is only meaningful read beside the orders line.

panels.title: Tokens per order
panels.description: The price-independent half of cost per order (capacity-plan A21 models ~333). This is the number a prompt change or a cache regression moves; the cost line also moves when a vendor reprices, which is not an engineering regression. Bounded for the same reason as the cost line: no placements in the window records +Inf.
